concept.name: Sharpe ratio
concept.definition: The ratio of a fund's average differential (excess) return over a benchmark or risk-free rate to the standard deviation of that differential return — the reward-to-variability measure introduced by William Sharpe in 1966 and generalized in his 1994 exposition. It summarizes expected (ex ante) or realized (ex post) return per unit of total risk.
concept.intuition: It answers: for each unit of volatility endured, how much return above the risk-free alternative did the strategy deliver? Higher means more efficient conversion of risk into return.
concept.mechanics: Compute the differential return series (fund minus benchmark or risk-free rate), take its mean and standard deviation over the sample, and divide; annualize by scaling the mean by the period count and sigma by its square root. The ratio is scale-independent — leverage changes mean and sigma proportionally — which is why it suits zero-investment strategies.
concept.formula: S = E[D] / sigma_D, where D_t = R_F,t - R_B,t is the differential return versus the benchmark or risk-free rate; annualized, S_ann = S_period * sqrt(P) for P periods per year.
concept.failure_modes: It uses only the first two moments, so skewed or fat-tailed strategies (option selling, carry) show inflated Sharpes until the tail event arrives; smoothed or stale marks on illiquid assets understate sigma and overstate the ratio. It is also time-scale dependent and assumes the differential returns are comparable across the sample.
concept.misconceptions: A high historical Sharpe is not a forecast — ex post ratios are noisy estimates of ex ante performance — and the numerator must be the differential (excess) return: dividing the raw return mean by sigma loses the measure's meaning.
concept.example: An annual excess return of 6% with 15% volatility gives a Sharpe ratio of 0.40 — Sharpe's own illustration of a developed-country stock market index.

citations.source: Sharpe, W. F.: The Sharpe Ratio (Journal of Portfolio Management, Fall 1994; author-hosted reprint, Stanford)
citations.section: The Ratio (ex ante and ex post definitions)
